title: Flower Drum Song in the Communist Party and on Broadway
summary: Jang compares the Flower Drum Song to the dozens, traces its use by the Communist Party and its Rodgers and Hammerstein adaptation, and worries about rambling.

story.theme_name: Medicine shows, minstrels, circuses and the black theater circuit
story.community_name: On the road with minstrel, carnival and tent shows

blocks.x: then I had gone through, to me, the change of tradition, the tradition of transformation in China. That “Flower Drum Song” became an important cultural device for the Chinese communist party to recruit illiterate peasants in the countryside. You’d have a performance of the “Flower Drum Song” that was something familiar to peasants to draw them in, and then later on, in 1945, [s/l] Yuan Nin, who was an actress from Shanghai and also a member of the communist party, performed it in, I think it was March of 1945 towards the end of Roosevelt’s days. I mean Roosevelt, President Roosevelt died I think in April of 1945. She performed the “Flower Drum Song.” And then we see that there was a novel in 195 — what was it, 7? — by C.Y. Lee, that was part of another lost generation, which was made into a Broadway musical by Rodgers & Hammerstein, and that was significant because it made a film in 1961 which was kind of loosely based on, or loosely inspired by Forbidden City, one of the early, but not the first, early Chinatown nightclubs in San Francisco. And so I mean why is that significant? Because there was no films that featured Asian-American actors in a very human way until 1992, I think it was Wayne Wang, “Joy Luck Club.” So that was significant about Rodgers & Hammerstein. If Hammerstein had lived, because he died I think around the release of the film in 1961, had he lived longer, who knows what could have happened. I know I’m getting — are you going to edit this?
Oh okay. Because that’s why I’m talking. Just try to tell me what you want me — to guide me. See I’m older now so now I’ve got the longer stories.
